text: The art of war is of vital importance to the State. It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin. Hence it is a subject of inquiry which can on no account be neglected.
The art of war is governed by five constant factors: the Moral Law, Heaven, Earth, the Commander, and Method and discipline.
All warfare is based on deception. When able to attack, seem unable. When using forces, seem inactive. When near, make it seem far. When far, make it seem near.
If your opponent is of choleric temper, seek to irritate them. Pretend to be weak, that they may grow arrogant. If they are taking their ease, give them no rest.
While heading the profit of my counsel, avail yourself also of any helpful circumstances over and beyond the ordinary rules. According as circumstances are favorable, one should modify one's plans.
He who knows when he can fight and when he cannot will be victorious. He who knows how to use both large and small forces will be victorious.
There is no instance of a nation benefiting from prolonged warfare. No country has ever benefited from a protracted war.
The skillful leader subdues the enemy's troops without any fighting. They capture the enemy's cities without laying siege to them, and overthrow the enemy's kingdom without prolonged operations.
The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting. The highest form of generalship is to balk the enemy's plans.
The wise commander avoids engaging superior forces. If equally matched, they may give battle; if slightly inferior, they avoid the enemy; if quite unequal, they flee.
Know your enemy and know yourself, and you will not be imperiled in a hundred battles. Know yourself but not your enemy, and you will suffer one defeat for every victory.
A victorious army wins its victories before seeking battle. A defeated army fights first and then seeks victory.
The good fighters of old first put themselves beyond the possibility of defeat, and then waited for an opportunity of defeating the enemy.
Invincibility lies in the defense. The possibility of victory lies in the attack. One defends when strength is inadequate; one attacks when it is abundant.
The victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won. One who is destined to defeat first fights and afterward looks for victory.
In battle, there are only two methods of attack — the direct and the indirect. Yet their combinations give rise to an endless series of maneuvers.
The direct and the indirect lead on to each other in turn. It is like moving in a circle — you never come to an end. Who can exhaust the possibilities of their combination?
The energy developed by good fighters is like the momentum of a round boulder rolled down a mountain. Such is the energy of perfect timing.
Whoever is first in the field and awaits the coming of the enemy will be fresh for the fight. Whoever is second in the field and must hasten to battle will arrive exhausted.
You can be sure of succeeding in your attacks if you only attack places that are undefended. You can ensure the safety of your defense if you only hold positions that cannot be attacked.
If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory gained you will also suffer a defeat.
The skillful commander can be relied on to lead his forces straight to the goal without losing men. March by the most direct route, and avoid the enemy when they are fresh and strong.
When you surround an army, leave an outlet free. Do not press a desperate foe too hard.
Throw your soldiers into positions whence there is no escape, and they will prefer death to flight. If they face death, there is nothing they cannot achieve.
The commander must adapt their plans to the situation. There are roads which must not be followed, armies which must not be attacked, towns which must not be besieged.
The commander who advances without seeking fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only aim is to protect the country — such a leader is a jewel of the state.
Armies must encamp in high ground, avoiding low-lying areas. They must face the sun and rely on dry ground. Good generals take care of their soldiers as they would their own children.
When the enemy's soldiers are standing leaning on their spears, they are faint from want of food. If those who are sent to draw water begin by drinking themselves, the army is suffering from thirst.
There are six types of terrain: accessible, entangling, temporizing, narrow, precipitous, and distant. The wise commander studies each carefully.
If you know your soldiers and can depend on their strength, but do not know the enemy, for every victory there will be a defeat. Knowledge of both is the path to victory.
There are nine varieties of ground on which armies operate: dispersive, frontier, key, open, focal, serious, difficult, encircled, and desperate.
When one treats people with benevolence and maintains good order, one commands their loyalty. When rewards and punishments are just, the army is well-disciplined.
The skillful commander moves as if from beneath the earth, then like thunder from above. They do not allow their plans to be known.
The attack by fire is a severe method. There are five ways of attacking with fire: burning soldiers, burning stores, burning equipment, burning arsenals, and burning lines of communication.
The enlightened commander is calm and just in their decisions. They take into account both the advantages and the dangers of every situation.
What enables a wise commander to know the enemy's situation in advance is intelligence. Not divination, not supernatural powers, but information from other people.
Knowledge of the enemy's disposition can only be obtained from other people. Spies are the most important element in war, for on them depends an army's ability to move.
It is the business of a general to be quiet and thus ensure secrecy, upright and just to maintain order. He must be able to mystify his officers and men by false reports.
An army without secret agents is like a man without eyes or ears. Spies are essential to know the enemy's condition and intentions.
